title: The Cost of Giving Crisis
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: An Australian secondary teacher diagnoses 'results inflation' -- the systemic tendency for student grades to be reported at or above curriculum level regardless of actual achievement -- and identifies four interlocking causes: the near-impossibility of having a student repeat a year, parental expectation of constant upward progress, teacher ignorance of what curriculum levels actually mean, and the implicit punishment of teachers whose students fail. The author documents the downstream harm: students who arrive at senior years with 80s on their transcripts unable to perform at that level, and teachers who follow the spec being questioned while colleagues who inflate face no scrutiny. The piece concludes that teachers are not the problem -- the systemic incentives are -- and calls for reform of reporting norms and teacher education on curriculum standards.
points: Results inflation compounds over time: students carrying inflated grades arrive at senior classes unable to perform at the level their transcripts claim, creating a jarring discontinuity that the receiving teacher has to manage while taking the blame.

Four systemic pressures push teachers toward grade inflation: (1) retention policies make failing a student practically impossible; (2) parents expect upward-only trajectories; (3) ITE rarely teaches teachers what curriculum levels actually mean; (4) a student failing in your class signals perceived poor teaching.

The 'multiple opportunities' policy -- designed to give students fair chances -- is frequently interpreted as 'keep giving tasks until you get a satisfactory result,' adding 5-10 hours of work per student and creating a workload incentive to just pass them the first time.

The most competent teachers are paradoxically most likely to report failures -- because they actually follow the spec -- and face the most scrutiny, while inflation-prone colleagues escape notice because their students always pass.

The author's proposed solution targets the system rather than individual teachers: better ITE curriculum training, clearer reporting expectations, and removal of the implicit penalty on teachers whose students fail.
quotes: Over the past decade I have noticed a steady decline in the prior knowledge that my students come to school with.

These same students come into my senior class and find that some of those 80's suddenly become 60's or sometimes even 40's. It is particularly curious when we are reporting against a state wide curriculum with set levels.

In my experience across over a decade of teaching, it is actually the most competent teachers who are most likely to report that a student has failed. They've usually followed all processes, jumped through all of the hoops and yet there will still often be comments made such as 'how do students always fail in your class when in Mr X's class over there every student is getting great grades?'
Just put them all at level unless they're really bright then put them 0.5 above or 0.5 below if they're struggling -- real staffroom commentary I've heard in reporting season.
If we punish teachers for maintaining high expectations and standards than we are just asking the whole staff to bury the bar so low in the ground that it is impossible not to clear.

Teachers are not the problem (they rarely are despite the venting sessions I sometimes have with my friends). It is the lack of education about reporting as well as the expectations we place on teachers that everybody needs to pass.
